lesson.title: Finding (f^-1)'(b) Without Ever Finding f^-1
lesson.summary: The Inverse Function Theorem lets you compute the derivative of an inverse function at a specific point using only values of f and f', even when no formula for the inverse exists.
lesson.body:
The real value of the Inverse Function Theorem, (f^{-1})'(b) = 1/f'(a) where b = f(a), is not just that it is true, it is that it lets you skip a step that is often impossible: writing down a formula for f^{-1} itself. All you need is one x-value a, the corresponding output b = f(a), and the ordinary derivative f'(a).

Take f(x) = x^3 + x + 1. First confirm f is invertible at all: f'(x) = 3x^2 + 1, and since 3x^2 is never negative, f'(x) is always at least 1, always positive, so f is strictly increasing everywhere and therefore one-to-one on the whole real line, guaranteeing an inverse exists (prerequisite: derivative function, used here to certify invertibility).

Now find (f^{-1})'(3). Look for an x-value where f(x) = 3: try x = 1, since f(1) = 1^3 + 1 + 1 = 3. That is the a you need. Compute f'(1) = 3(1)^2 + 1 = 4. By the theorem, (f^{-1})'(3) = 1/f'(1) = 1/4.

Notice what was never needed: an explicit formula for f^{-1}(x). Solving x^3 + x + 1 = y for x in general requires the full cubic formula, which is unwieldy and not something you would want to differentiate directly. Yet the derivative of the inverse at this one point came out in two short lines, using only a value of f and a value of f'. This is exactly why the theorem matters as a working tool, not just as a piece of theory.
